$schema_note: Phase 0 proof-of-concept dataset for the billionaire-government-money profile (docs/ideas/billionaire-subsidy-tracker.md). Subject is a named living family: every figure is source-linked. The unit of truth is the COMPANY (Walmart) and the AWARD; the FAMILY is a lens (Sam Walton founded Walmart; his heirs Rob, Jim, and Alice Walton plus their family entities hold ~45% of Walmart's shares and control it). The Walton case is STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT from the Musk/Bezos cases: those empires are powered by federal CONTRACTS (the government buying launches, cloud, logistics). Walmart's government money is overwhelmingly (a) direct state/local SUBSIDIES to site stores and distribution centers, and (b) INDIRECT / STRUCTURAL public money — SNAP benefits spent at Walmart registers (demand-side), and public assistance (Medicaid/SNAP) flowing to Walmart's low-wage workers (a cost of low wages, NOT a payment to Walmart). These structural figures are CONTESTED and must NEVER be summed with direct subsidies into a single 'the Waltons got $X' number. Money TYPE values: FEDERAL_CONTRACT, FEDERAL_GRANT, FEDERAL_LOAN, TAX_CREDIT_SUBSIDY, STATE_LOCAL_SUBSIDY, REGULATORY_CREDIT, POLITICAL_SPENDING. POLITICAL_SPENDING is money flowing OUT from Walmart/the Waltons, tracked for the side-by-side, and is NOT government money received.
subject: The Walton family / Walmart

headline.label: at least ~$1 billion (direct state & local subsidies)
headline.description: The cleanest HARD figure: Walmart has captured at least ~$1 billion in documented state and local economic-development subsidies (tax abatements, free/discounted land, infrastructure, training grants, tax-increment financing) to site its stores and distribution centers, per Good Jobs First — which found 244 Walmart stores and distribution centers in 35+ states receiving subsidies totaling just over $1 billion, with more than 90% of Walmart's distribution centers subsidized. This is the only category that is unambiguously money/value transferred TO Walmart by government. It is deliberately NOT the headline-grabbing structural figures (SNAP revenue, worker public assistance) below, which are indirect and contested.
headline.composition: Direct state & local subsidies to 244+ Walmart stores and distribution centers across 35+ states — property/sales-tax abatements, free or discounted land, infrastructure assistance, tax-increment financing, enterprise-zone tax credits, and job-training grants. Excludes the much larger but INDIRECT structural figures (SNAP register revenue, worker public assistance) tracked separately in the line items.
headline.time_period: cumulative through Good Jobs First's tally (original 'Shopping for Subsidies' study 2004; figure has only grown since)
caveats: This is a FLOOR. Good Jobs First states the true total is 'undoubtedly much higher' than the documented ~$1B because many local deals are never disclosed. The live Subsidy Tracker parent-company page (subsidytracker.goodjobsfirst.org/parent/walmart) carries the running total but is access-gated to automated fetch.

The ~$1B is the ONLY figure here that is direct government-to-Walmart value. It must NOT be conflated with — or summed with — the SNAP-revenue (~$13-20B/yr) or worker-public-assistance (~$6.2B/yr) figures, which are demand-side / structural and not handouts to Walmart.

Walmart is a publicly traded company; subsidies benefit all shareholders (pension funds, index investors, millions of small holders), not just the Waltons. The family controls ~45% of shares — attribution is family-CONTROL-based, not a wire transfer to a personal account.
Subsidy values are often ANNOUNCED/authorized multi-year package values, not realized cash; realized value differs and is frequently disputed.

line_items.time_period: cumulative (Good Jobs First 'Shopping for Subsidies', 2004 baseline; ongoing)
line_items.description: Documented state and local economic-development subsidies to Walmart stores and distribution centers: property- and sales-tax abatements, free or discounted land, site/infrastructure assistance, tax-increment financing (TIF), enterprise-zone credits, and job-training grants. Good Jobs First identified 244 subsidized Walmart stores and distribution centers across 35+ states; more than 90% of Walmart distribution centers received subsidies.
line_items.agency: Multiple state & local governments (per Good Jobs First Subsidy Tracker)
line_items.value_basis: compiled tally of disclosed deals; floor figure — GJF says true total is higher; live running total on the gated Subsidy Tracker parent page
line_items.notes: This is the headline figure. The cleanest, least-contested category: government value transferred directly TO Walmart to site facilities. The live parent-company page (subsidytracker.goodjobsfirst.org/parent/walmart) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; the ~$1B+ figure is taken from GJF's own 'Shopping for Subsidies' study and ILSR's corroborating summary.

line_items.category: SNAP revenue captured (demand-side, NOT a handout to Walmart)
line_items.amount_label: ~$13 billion/yr (2013, last officially disclosed); estimated ~$20B+/yr more recently
line_items.time_period: per-year; $13B figure is for 2013 (last year Walmart disclosed); Numerator put Walmart's SNAP share at 25.8% for the 12 months ending July 2024
line_items.description: Government money (SNAP / food-stamp benefits) spent BY SHOPPERS at Walmart registers. Walmart redeems roughly a quarter of ALL U.S. SNAP dollars: ~18% (~$13B) in 2013 per Walmart's own last disclosure, and 25.8% of SNAP shoppers' grocery dollars over the 12 months ending July 2024 per Numerator's SNAP Shopper Scorecard (94.3% of SNAP recipients shop at Walmart). Moody's has estimated Walmart's annual SNAP sales exceed $20 billion.
line_items.agency: USDA (SNAP) — benefits spent by recipients, redeemed by Walmart as an authorized retailer
line_items.value_basis: 2013 figure is Walmart's own disclosure (~$13B, ~18% of SNAP); 25.8% share is Numerator (12 mo. ending July 2024); ~$20B+/yr is Moody's estimate. USDA does not publish per-retailer SNAP redemption totals (subject of years of litigation/FOIA fights).
line_items.critical_nuance: DEMAND-SIDE / STRUCTURAL. This is taxpayer money flowing INTO Walmart's registers, but it is benefits SPENT BY SHOPPERS who choose Walmart — Walmart earns it as a retailer selling groceries, exactly as a grocery store earns any customer's dollar. It is NOT a subsidy, grant, or handout paid TO Walmart by the government. Listing it as 'government money to the Waltons' without this framing is misleading. It must NEVER be summed with the direct ~$1B subsidy headline. Typed FEDERAL_GRANT only because SNAP is a federal program; functionally it is program-driven retail revenue.
line_items.notes: USDA has refused (and litigated) to release per-retailer SNAP redemption data, so exact current Walmart totals are not officially knowable; figures are disclosures/estimates.

line_items.category: Hidden taxpayer subsidy of low wages (structural, contested)
line_items.time_period: estimate published 2014 (Americans for Tax Fairness), based on 2012-2013 data; widely cited since, including by Bernie Sanders 2018
line_items.description: Estimated annual cost to U.S. taxpayers of public-assistance programs (SNAP, Medicaid, subsidized housing, EITC, etc.) used by Walmart's low-wage workers — framed by critics as taxpayers subsidizing Walmart's low pay. Americans for Tax Fairness estimated ~$6.2 billion/yr by taking the midpoint of per-employee cost estimates (derived from a 2013 U.S. House Education & Workforce Committee Democratic-staff report using Wisconsin Medicaid data) and scaling to Walmart's ~1.4M U.S. workforce.
line_items.agency: Multiple federal/state programs (Medicaid, SNAP, housing, EITC) — paid to WORKERS, not to Walmart
line_items.value_basis: extrapolated estimate (single-state Medicaid data scaled to national workforce); PolitiFact and others have flagged the $6.2B as an old, methodologically rough figure
line_items.critical_nuance: HIGHLY CONTESTED, INDIRECT, STRUCTURAL — the most-attacked number in this dataset. This is public assistance paid to Walmart's EMPLOYEES because their wages are low; NOT money paid to Walmart. Treating it as 'Walmart got $6.2B' is a category error: it is a cost society bears, framed by critics as an implicit subsidy of Walmart's wage structure. The methodology (one state's Medicaid data extrapolated nationally) is rough; PolitiFact rated Sanders' 2018 reuse of it as relying on a dated figure. The 2020 GAO report (GAO-21-45) is the firmer corroboration: it found Walmart among the TOP FOUR employers of SNAP and Medicaid enrollees in EVERY state studied (top employer of SNAP recipients in 5 of 9 states; top Medicaid-enrollee employer in 3 of 6 states) — but GAO did NOT attach a dollar figure to Walmart specifically. MUST NEVER be summed with the direct subsidy headline.
line_items.notes: Walmart has since raised starting wages (to $14+/hr average in recent years), which it argues reduces this figure; critics argue it remains material. The $6.2B is best presented as a contested 2014-era estimate, with GAO-21-45 as the rigorous (but dollar-less) confirmation that Walmart's workforce disproportionately relies on public aid.

line_items.amount_label: no clean cumulative total; tens of millions/yr in government card purchases; GSA e-commerce portal participant
line_items.description: Walmart's DIRECT federal contracting is small relative to its empire. It is among the top five big-box retailers selling to the U.S. government; government employees spent tens of millions of dollars at Walmart via GSA SmartPay purchase cards (the government spent ~$74M across Walmart and peer retailers via cards in 2018), and Walmart was selected for the GSA Commercial Platforms (e-commerce portal) program for federal micro-purchases under $10K. Walmart also holds federal pharmacy reimbursement (Medicare Part D / Medicaid) revenue, not itemized here.
line_items.agency: GSA (SmartPay, Commercial Platforms) + various federal buyers
line_items.value_basis: no consolidated public Walmart federal-contract total; card-spending and portal participation are documented but not aggregated to a single Walmart figure
line_items.notes: Included for completeness to show the CONTRAST with Musk/Bezos: unlike SpaceX (NASA/DoD contracts) or Amazon (AWS/JEDI/JWCC cloud), Walmart is NOT a major federal contractor. Its government money is subsidies + structural retail revenue, not procurement. USAspending.gov would carry any prime awards; no large aggregate is publicly compiled.

line_items.category: Political spending (money OUT, not government money received)
line_items.description: Walmart Inc. PAC for Responsible Government (FEC C00093054) federal contributions: $2,627,025 across 1,653 transactions through Sept 30, 2024 (OpenSecrets lists $1,157,500 to federal candidates for the full cycle). Walmart's corporate giving favored Republicans roughly 2-to-1.
line_items.value_basis: FEC filings (PAC C00093054); candidate-recipient total per OpenSecrets
line_items.notes: NOT government money received — this is Walmart spending. The $2.63M (transactions) and $1.16M (to candidates) differ because the latter is only direct candidate contributions; the former includes contributions to other committees.

line_items.description: Seven Walton heirs gave $21,990,900 across 186 transactions in the 2024 cycle. Combined with Walmart's corporate PAC, Walmart and the Waltons invested over $32 million in direct political spending; the family favored Republicans by more than 13-to-1, and over $22 million flowed into nominally 'non-partisan' issue PACs funding largely conservative causes.
line_items.value_basis: United for Respect tally of FEC filings; individual contributions are FEC-traceable
line_items.notes: NOT government money received. Family political giving is SEPARATE from the Walton Family Foundation's philanthropy (next item). The combined Walmart-PAC + Walton-family $32M is the headline political figure.

line_items.category: Philanthropy / advocacy (NOT political-PAC money, NOT government money)
line_items.amount_label: $1 billion over 5 years (announced K-12 / charter-school plan); >$1B cumulative to date
line_items.time_period: charter funding since 1996; the $1B/5yr plan announced ~2016; ongoing
line_items.description: The Walton Family Foundation is one of the largest private funders of charter schools and school-choice advocacy in the U.S. — it has helped fund roughly 1 in 4 U.S. charter-school startups since 1996 and committed $1 billion over five years to K-12 education reform. Recent vehicles include a $400M Facilities Investment Fund (with PNC Bank and Civic Builders).
line_items.agency: N/A (private philanthropy / 501(c)(3) foundation; influences education policy)
line_items.value_basis: foundation announcements; cumulative education giving exceeds $1B
line_items.notes: CRITICAL: This is PHILANTHROPY, not FEC political-PAC money and NOT government money received. It is included to document the family's policy influence (school-choice/charter advocacy), which is a form of political influence distinct from campaign contributions. Typed POLITICAL_SPENDING (money OUT, influence) for the side-by-side, but it is charitable giving — do not conflate with the FEC figures above or with any 'government money to the Waltons' total. Methodology note: in the Common Ground frame, Walton Foundation charter/voucher advocacy is exactly the school-privatization push that Plank 2 ('no vouchers/charters') is positioned against.

caveats:
CRITICAL DISTINCTIONS (read before citing any number) — the Walton case is fundamentally different from the contract-driven Musk/Bezos cases:

1. THERE IS NO SINGLE CLEAN 'THE WALTONS GOT $X' NUMBER. The honest headline is the ~$1 billion in documented direct STATE & LOCAL SUBSIDIES to Walmart stores/distribution centers (Good Jobs First). That is the ONLY category that is unambiguously government value transferred TO Walmart. Everything else below is either INDIRECT (SNAP register revenue), STRUCTURAL/CONTESTED (worker public assistance), or money flowing OUT (political spending, philanthropy). NEVER sum these into one figure.

2. SNAP REVENUE IS DEMAND-SIDE, NOT A HANDOUT. Walmart redeems ~a quarter of all U.S. SNAP dollars (~$13B in 2013, the last official disclosure; 25.8% share per Numerator for the year ending July 2024; ~$20B+/yr per Moody's). This is taxpayer money landing in Walmart's registers — but it is benefits SPENT BY SHOPPERS who choose Walmart, exactly as any grocer earns a customer's dollar. It is program-driven RETAIL REVENUE, not a subsidy, grant, or check written to Walmart. Presenting it as 'government money to the Waltons' without this framing is misleading. USDA has litigated to keep per-retailer SNAP totals secret, so exact current figures are not officially knowable.

3. WORKER PUBLIC ASSISTANCE IS THE MOST-CONTESTED NUMBER. The ~$6.2 billion/yr 'hidden taxpayer subsidy' (Americans for Tax Fairness, 2014) is public assistance — Medicaid, SNAP, housing — paid to Walmart's low-wage EMPLOYEES, NOT to Walmart. It is a cost society bears, framed by critics as taxpayers subsidizing Walmart's low pay. The estimate is methodologically rough (one state's Medicaid data scaled to a 1.4M national workforce) and dated; PolitiFact has flagged its reuse. The 2020 GAO report GAO-21-45 is the rigorous corroboration — Walmart is among the top four employers of SNAP/Medicaid enrollees in every state GAO studied — but GAO attached NO dollar figure to Walmart. Treat $6.2B as a contested, low-confidence, structural estimate; never sum it with anything.

4. DEMAND-SIDE vs SUPPLY-SIDE. Both the big structural figures are DEMAND-SIDE: SNAP benefits are spent by shoppers; Medicaid/SNAP for workers is paid to workers. Neither is a supply-side payment TO Walmart. The ~$1B direct subsidy is the only supply-side, to-the-company figure.

5. WALMART IS BARELY A FEDERAL CONTRACTOR. Unlike SpaceX (NASA/DoD launches) or Amazon (AWS cloud), Walmart's direct federal procurement is small — GSA SmartPay card purchases (tens of millions/yr across big-box peers) and the GSA Commercial Platforms e-commerce portal. There is no large, compiled Walmart federal-contract total. This is the core contrast: Musk/Bezos money is CONTRACTS (government buying things); Walton money is SUBSIDIES + STRUCTURAL retail/labor flows.

6. THE WALTONS ARE HEIRS, NOT THE FOUNDER, AND WALMART IS PUBLIC. Sam Walton founded Walmart (d. 1992); his heirs — Rob, Jim, and Alice Walton, plus Walton Enterprises and the Walton Family Holdings Trust — hold ~45% of shares (Walton Enterprises 44.21% + the family trust 6.53% on the relevant filings) and control the company. Attribution is FAMILY-CONTROL-based. But Walmart is publicly traded: subsidies and revenue also benefit pension funds, index funds, and millions of small shareholders. The dollars went to the COMPANY; the family controls and benefits from ~45% of it. It is analytically false to imply any of this landed in a Walton personal bank account.

7. GROSS REVENUE != SUBSIDY != PROFIT != PERSONAL WEALTH. SNAP register revenue is gross sales (most of it is cost of goods); a subsidy/tax break is forgone public revenue; neither is profit; and none is the family's ~$350B+ personal net worth (which is share value, driven by markets, not a pile of government cash). Keep these four planes separate.

8. POLITICAL SPENDING & PHILANTHROPY ARE MONEY OUT, NOT MONEY IN. The Walmart PAC ($2.63M), Walton heirs ($21.99M; >$32M combined), and Walton Family Foundation charter giving (>$1B) are money the family/company SPENT — on politics and on policy advocacy — included for the side-by-side contrast (public money received vs. influence purchased). They are NOT government money received and must never be added to the subsidy figures. Foundation giving is charitable, not FEC-reported political money — keep it distinct from the PAC figures too.

9. AGGREGATES & ESTIMATES. Several figures are estimates or ranges (SNAP $13B-$20B+; worker aid $6.2B; subsidies 'at least ~$1B, undoubtedly higher'). Confidence is labeled per line. For any total, use ONLY the ~$1B direct-subsidy headline (a floor), and present the structural figures as separate, clearly-labeled context — never a single blended sum.
